title: Ask for a Raise or Switch Jobs? The 10-Year Math
description:
Should you stay for yearly raises or switch jobs for a bigger bump? In this example, two people start on $60,000. Staying with 3% raises reaches about $78K in year ten; switching every three years for a 10% bump reaches about $95K, about $62K more earned over the decade.

Real raises are often smaller. In the Atlanta Fed's Wage Growth Tracker (data to September 2026), median pay growth was 4.7% a year for job switchers vs 3.4% for people who stayed. Using those numbers in the same example, the 10-year gap shrinks to about $11K.

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Wage Growth Tracker (3-month moving average of median wage growth, released Oct 8, 2026): https://www.atlantafed.org/chcs/wage-growth-tracker

Example assumptions (real raises vary by job, field and year): $60,000 starting salary, 3% yearly raise when staying, 10% raise at each switch in years 4, 7 and 10 and 3% in the other years, no gaps between jobs, salary only (no bonuses, benefits or retirement matching). Switching has costs too: risk, a learning curve and benefits you may lose. This is not career or financial advice.

scenes.say: In this example, staying loyal costs about sixty-two thousand dollars over ten years. Here's the math, and the catch.
Two people start at sixty thousand dollars. Sara stays and gets three percent a year. Leo switches every three years for a ten percent bump.
Each switch resets Leo's pay higher. By year ten, Sara earns about seventy-eight thousand; Leo, about ninety-five thousand.
Over the decade, Leo earns about sixty-two thousand dollars more.

But real bumps are often smaller. In US data, switchers' pay recently grew four point seven percent a year, versus three point four for stayers. At those rates, Leo's lead shrinks to about eleven thousand.
